questions.prompt: Why is constructor injection generally preferred over field injection?
options: Dependencies can be final, are explicit, and the class can be instantiated in plain unit tests without reflection
Field injection is removed in Spring 6
questions.explanation: With a single constructor, @Autowired is optional. Field injection hides dependencies and requires a container or reflection to test.

questions.prompt: A @Service method a() calls this.b(), where b() is annotated @Transactional. Does b() get a transaction when called this way?
options: No; the call bypasses the Spring proxy, so the annotation's advice doesn't run
questions.explanation: Spring AOP proxies intercept calls coming from outside the bean. Fixes include moving b() to another bean, or restructuring so the transactional boundary is the public entry point.

questions.prompt: What is the default scope of a Spring bean?
questions.explanation: Because singletons are shared across threads, they should be stateless or thread-safe.

questions.prompt: Which status code fits a successful POST that creates a resource?
questions.explanation: 202 means the work was accepted but not finished (asynchronous). 204 means success with no body, common for DELETE.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
options: 401: not authenticated (who are you?); 403: authenticated but not allowed
questions.explanation: Some APIs return 404 instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a resource exists.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP methods are defined as idempotent?
questions.explanation: Repeating an idempotent request has the same effect as sending it once. POST is not idempotent, so payment APIs use idempotency keys to make retries safe.

questions.prompt: What's the purpose of @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods?
options: To centralise mapping of exceptions to consistent HTTP error responses across controllers
questions.explanation: This keeps controllers clean and stops internal details such as stack traces from leaking into responses.

questions.prompt: Where does Spring Security perform authentication and authorization for servlet requests?
options: In a chain of servlet filters (SecurityFilterChain) before the request reaches DispatcherServlet
questions.explanation: DelegatingFilterProxy hands requests to FilterChainProxy, which selects the matching SecurityFilterChain. Method security such as @PreAuthorize adds checks at the service layer.

questions.prompt: When is CSRF protection most important?
options: For stateless APIs using bearer tokens in an Authorization header
When the browser automatically sends credentials, such as session cookies, with cross-site requests
questions.explanation: CSRF exploits ambient credentials. Cookie-based sessions need CSRF tokens and/or SameSite cookies. Safe methods (GET) must not change state.

questions.prompt: Which is appropriate for storing user passwords?
options: A slow, salted, adaptive hash such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2
AES encryption with a server key
questions.explanation: Fast hashes are easy to brute-force offline on GPUs. Adaptive algorithms have a tunable work factor and per-password salts.

questions.prompt: Loading 50 orders and then accessing each order's lazy customer triggers 51 queries. What is this and a common fix?
options: The N+1 select problem; fetch the association in the query (JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph) or use batch fetching
A cache miss; enable the second-level cache
questions.explanation: Each lazy proxy initialisation issues its own SELECT. Fetching only what the use case needs, or projecting into DTOs, avoids it.

questions.prompt: Inside a @Transactional method you load an entity and call a setter, without calling save(). What happens at commit?
options: The change is flushed automatically because managed entities are dirty-checked
The change is saved only if the entity is new
questions.explanation: The persistence context tracks managed entities and generates an UPDATE for those that changed. Detached entities are not tracked.

questions.prompt: Why do many teams disable spring.jpa.open-in-view?
options: It keeps a persistence context, and often a DB connection, open through view rendering, hiding lazy-loading queries outside the service layer
questions.explanation: Disabling it forces explicit fetching inside transactional services, which makes query counts visible and frees connections sooner.

questions.prompt: How does @Version-based optimistic locking detect a lost update?
options: It locks the row on read
The UPDATE includes WHERE version = ?; if no row matches, someone else changed it, and an optimistic lock exception is thrown
questions.explanation: It needs no lock while reading. It suits low-contention workloads, where the client can retry or show a conflict.

questions.prompt: By default, does a @Transactional method roll back when it throws a checked exception?
options: No; by default only RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback
questions.explanation: Use @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) when checked exceptions should roll back too.

questions.prompt: What does Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW do when called from inside an existing transaction?
options: Suspends the outer transaction and runs in a new, independent one that commits or rolls back on its own
questions.explanation: This is useful for audit logs that must survive an outer rollback. It needs a second connection, which matters with small pools. NESTED uses savepoints instead.

questions.prompt: What can @Transactional(readOnly = true) do?
options: Prevent all writes at the database level in every case
Hint to the provider and driver to optimise (e.g. Hibernate skips dirty checking/flush) for read-only work
Make queries faster by caching them
questions.explanation: Whether the database itself enforces read-only depends on the driver and configuration. It is primarily an optimisation and intent hint.

questions.prompt: What does @Cacheable("products") on a method do?
options: Returns a cached result for the same arguments if present; otherwise invokes the method and stores the result
questions.explanation: Use @CacheEvict or @CachePut to keep the cache consistent on writes. Like @Transactional, it relies on proxies, so self-invocation bypasses it.

questions.prompt: Why might an in-memory cache (e.g. Caffeine) cause inconsistency when the app runs on 3 instances?
options: Each instance has its own cache, so an eviction on one instance doesn't evict on the others
questions.explanation: Options are short TTLs, a shared cache such as Redis, or broadcasting invalidations between instances.

questions.prompt: What does @WebMvcTest load?
options: The full application context and database
Only the web layer (controllers, advice, filters, converters); services must be mocked
questions.explanation: Slice tests start faster and focus on one layer. Use @SpringBootTest for full integration tests, ideally against a real database.

questions.prompt: Why test repositories against real PostgreSQL rather than H2?
options: Dialect differences (e.g. JSONB, arrays, partial indexes, locking behaviour) mean H2 can pass tests that fail in production
questions.explanation: Tools like Testcontainers or embedded PostgreSQL run the real engine in tests.

questions.prompt: When is a modular monolith usually a better starting point than microservices?
options: For a small team and a young product: you get module boundaries without network calls, distributed transactions or many deployments
questions.explanation: Microservices trade in-process simplicity for independent deployment and scaling, which pays off with team or scale pressure. Good module boundaries make a later split easier.

questions.prompt: Without a distributed transaction, how does a saga keep an order flow across services consistent?
options: A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails
questions.explanation: Sagas can be orchestrated (a central coordinator) or choreographed (services react to events). They give eventual consistency, so intermediate states are visible.
